document.title: Black-Box Uselessness: Composing Separations in Cryptography

candidate.title: Black-Box Helpfulness of One-Way Functions for Collision Resistance
candidate.subtitle: the existence of an auxiliary primitive that only works with a one-way function
candidate.one_line: Conjecturally there is a primitive that cannot build collision-resistant hashing on its own but can once a one-way function is added, so one-way functions are not useless for collision resistance even though they cannot produce it alone.
candidate.informal: Simon showed that collision-resistant hash functions cannot be built from one-way functions in a black-box way, by exhibiting a random permutation together with an oracle that returns collisions for any circuit built from it: relative to that pair, one-way permutations exist but collision-resistant hashing does not. This paper asks the sharper question of whether one-way functions are entirely useless for collision resistance, meaning that no auxiliary primitive is ever made sufficient for collision resistance by adding a one-way function to it. The authors conjecture the opposite. That is, they conjecture that there exists some auxiliary primitive from which collision-resistant hashing cannot be built in a black-box way, but from which, together with an arbitrary one-way function, it can. This would exhibit the first natural inhabitant of the gray zone between separation and uselessness, and would explain why one-way functions might yet play a role in future constructions of collision resistance from apparently weaker ingredients. The paper describes why proving it looks hard: Simon's result is an oracle separation and it is unclear how to relativize it, and the concrete candidate auxiliary primitive the authors propose reduces the conjecture to an unproved statement about the simultaneous hardness of inverting a one-way function and a random permutation.
candidate.definitions_latex:
\begin{definition}[Cryptographic primitive]
A \emph{cryptographic primitive} is a pair $\mathcal P=(F_{\mathcal P},R_{\mathcal P})$, where $F_{\mathcal P}$ is the set of functions \emph{implementing} $\mathcal P$ and $R_{\mathcal P}$ is a relation; for $\mathsf P\in F_{\mathcal P}$, $(\mathsf P,A)\in R_{\mathcal P}$ means the adversary $A$ \emph{breaks} $\mathsf P$. At least one $\mathsf P\in F_{\mathcal P}$ must be computable by a PPT algorithm.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Joint primitive]
Given $\mathcal P=(F_{\mathcal P},R_{\mathcal P})$ and $\mathcal Q=(F_{\mathcal Q},R_{\mathcal Q})$, the joint primitive $(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)$ has implementations $F_{\mathcal P}\times F_{\mathcal Q}$, and $((\mathsf P,\mathsf Q),(A_{\mathcal P},A_{\mathcal Q}))$ lies in its breaking relation iff $(\mathsf P,A_{\mathcal P})\in R_{\mathcal P}$ or $(\mathsf Q,A_{\mathcal Q})\in R_{\mathcal Q}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fully black-box reduction]
A \emph{fully black-box reduction} of a primitive $\mathcal P$ to a primitive $\mathcal Q$ is a pair $(\mathsf P,\mathsf S)$ of oracle-aided PPT machines such that for every implementation $\mathsf Q\in F_{\mathcal Q}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item (implementation reduction) $\mathsf P^{\mathsf Q}\in F_{\mathcal P}$; and
\item (security reduction) for every function $A$ with $(\mathsf P^{\mathsf Q},A)\in R_{\mathcal P}$, it holds that $(\mathsf Q,\mathsf S^{\mathsf Q,A})\in R_{\mathcal Q}$.
\end{itemize}
We say $\mathcal Q$ \emph{fully black-box implies} $\mathcal P$ if such a pair exists.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fully black-box helpfulness]
A primitive $\mathcal Q$ is \emph{fully black-box helpful} for a primitive $\mathcal P$ if there exists an auxiliary primitive $\mathcal Z$ such that the joint primitive $(\mathcal Q,\mathcal Z)$ fully black-box implies $\mathcal P$, yet $\mathcal Z$ alone does not fully black-box imply $\mathcal P$. (This is the negation of $\mathcal Q$ being fully black-box useless for $\mathcal P$.)
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[One-way functions]
The primitive $\mathcal F$ of one-way functions has as implementations all functions $\mathsf F$, and an adversary $A$ breaks $\mathsf F$ if there is a polynomial $p$ such that for infinitely many $\lambda\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\Pr_{x\gets\{0,1\}^{\lambda}}\big[\mathsf F\big(A(1^{\lambda},\mathsf F(x))\big)=\mathsf F(x)\big]\ \ge\ \frac{1}{p(\lambda)} .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Collision-resistant hash functions]
The primitive $\mathcal{CRH}$ has as implementations all functions $\mathsf H$ mapping a key $k\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}$ and an input $x\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}$ to $\mathsf H(k,x)\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}$, and an adversary $A$ breaks $\mathsf H$ if there is a polynomial $p$ such that for infinitely many $\lambda\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\Pr_{k\gets\{0,1\}^{\lambda}}\big[(x,x')\gets A(1^{\lambda},k)\;:\;x\neq x'\ \wedge\ \mathsf H(k,x)=\mathsf H(k,x')\big]\ \ge\ \frac{1}{p(\lambda)} .
\]
\end{definition}

parameters.meaning: the auxiliary primitive whose existence is asserted; the whole content of the conjecture is that some such primitive exists
the primitive of collision-resistant hash functions

candidate.setting_latex:
Simon \cite{Sim98} separated collision-resistant hash functions from one-way functions (indeed from one-way permutations) by exhibiting a pair of oracles $(\pi,\mathsf{Coll}^{\pi})$, where $\pi$ is a random permutation and $\mathsf{Coll}^{\pi}$ takes as input a circuit with $\pi$-gates and returns a random collision for it, relative to which one-way permutations exist but collision-resistant hashing does not. This paper studies whether such separations \emph{compose}: a primitive $\mathcal Q$ is called black-box useless for $\mathcal P$ if adding $\mathcal Q$ to \emph{any} auxiliary primitive never enables a black-box construction of $\mathcal P$ that the auxiliary primitive did not already enable, and black-box helpful otherwise. The compiling-out separations and the transcript-sampling separations treated elsewhere in the paper do lift to uselessness; Simon's oracle separation, the authors observe, does not obviously lift, since it is not clear how to relativize an oracle separation of this kind. They conjecture that this failure is inherent, and that one-way functions are in fact helpful for collision resistance.

The gray zone between separation and uselessness is known to be non-empty, but only for artificial reasons: taking the joint primitive consisting of a collision-resistant hash function and a trapdoor permutation, neither component alone black-box implies the pair (using \cite{IR89} in one direction and Fischlin \cite{Fis02} in the other), yet each is trivially helpful for it. A proof of this conjecture would give the first natural example, and, as the paper stresses, would be an indication of why one-way functions could feature in future black-box constructions of collision resistance from seemingly weaker assumptions.

The paper offers two routes. The first takes the candidate auxiliary primitive to be Simon's pair $(\pi,\mathsf{Coll}^{\pi})$ itself, and uses the result of Holmgren and Lombardi \cite{HL18} that exponentially secure one-way \emph{product} functions black-box imply collision-resistant hashing; making this work requires showing that for every one-way function $\mathsf F$ the pair $(\mathsf F,(\pi,\mathsf{Coll}^{\pi}))$ is product one-way, which the authors could not prove. The second route uses the backdoored random oracle model of Bauer, Farshim and Mazaheri \cite{BFM18}, whose leakage oracle is strong enough to implement Simon's collision finder and where two independent instances combine into a collision-resistant hash function under a communication-complexity conjecture. Because a single conjecture about Simon's oracle cannot be pushed through for arbitrary primitives, the paper also formulates two relaxations of the conjecture, one using distributional black-box reductions (which need only work for a measure-one set of implementations) and one using class reductions in the sense of Shaltiel \cite{Sha20} (which need only work for efficient implementations), and proves that both follow from that conjecture. Reduction terminology throughout follows \cite{RTV04}.
candidate.status_note: Entirely open. The paper proves that two relaxations of it (distributional black-box helpfulness and class helpfulness) follow from an unproved amplification conjecture about Simon's oracle, but neither the relaxations nor that conjecture are established, and the complementary statement that one-way functions are black-box useless for collision resistance is also open.
candidate.progress_note: Theorem 6.8 shows that the distributional relaxation (Conjecture 6.5) follows from the amplification conjecture about Simon's oracle (Conjecture 6.7); Theorem 6.12 shows the class-reduction relaxation (Conjecture 6.11) follows from the same conjecture, using a Borel-Cantelli argument over the countable class of efficient one-way functions to extract a single auxiliary implementation that works for all of them. Section 6.4 records a second, independent route via backdoored random oracles, conditional on a communication-complexity conjecture from BFM18.
candidate.why_interesting: Black-box separations are the standard currency for saying a primitive is too weak to build another, and the community has accumulated many of them; almost nothing is known about whether they survive the addition of a second primitive. This conjecture claims the most-studied such separation, Simon's, does not survive: one-way functions really do help build collision resistance, they just cannot do it alone. Settling it either way reshapes how separation results should be read. A proof would also be the first natural inhabitant of the gray zone between separation and uselessness, and a refutation would mean Simon's oracle separation composes, which would be a strong and surprising strengthening of a twenty-five-year-old result.
candidate.why_clean: The statement is a single existential over auxiliary primitives, on top of the standard notion of a fully black-box reduction and the standard notions of one-way function and collision-resistant hash function. There is a concrete candidate for the auxiliary primitive, namely Simon's random permutation together with its collision finder, so a prover has somewhere definite to start; and the paper reduces two natural weakenings of the statement to one self-contained hardness conjecture about that candidate.
candidate.risks: (1) The paper does not give a formal definition of collision-resistant hash functions in its preliminaries (Section 2.2 defines one-way functions, key agreement and obfuscation only), so the $\mathcal{CRH}$ definition above is a standard keyed formalization supplied by me; a reviewer should check that nothing in the conjecture turns on keyed versus unkeyed, or on the compression ratio. (2) The paper says of Section 6 that it maintains "a relatively informal discussion", so the primitive-level unfolding of "fully black-box helpful" above, though it matches the paper's own informal definition and its formal distributional analogue (Definition 6.4), is a reconstruction. (3) Refuting the conjecture means proving that one-way functions are fully black-box useless for collision resistance, which is a strong statement; a would-be refuter should be clear which direction they are attacking. (4) I am not aware of a resolution since January 2021, but I have not exhaustively surveyed follow-up work on one-way product functions or on Simon's oracle.

quotes.text: One-way functions are fully black-box helpful for collision-resistant hash functions.

At first sight, it is not clear how one would extend Simon’s strategy to prove that one-way functions are BBU for CRHFs. In fact, we believe that this is inherent: we conjecture that the answer to the above question is no.
While we believe that Conjecture 6.1 holds, proving it seems quite challenging.

Formally, we call primitive Q black-box helpful (BBH) for P, if there exists an auxiliary primitive Z such that there exists a black-box construction of P from (Q, Z), but there exists no black-box construction of P from Z alone.
Indeed, we conjecture the opposite: OWFs are black-box helpful for building CRHFs.

Towards getting a better understanding of its plausibility, we introduce two natural relaxations of the conjecture, and show that each of these natural relaxations would follow from a plausible conjecture regarding Simon’s oracle, which might be of independent interest.

checks.name: Existence
checks.finding: Conjecture 6.1 appears verbatim on PDF p.29 (printed 27): "One-way functions are fully black-box helpful for collision-resistant hash functions." It is foreshadowed in the abstract (p.1, "We put forth the conjecture that one-way functions are black-box helpful for building collision-resistant hash functions") and in §1.5 (p.7, "Indeed, we conjecture the opposite: OWFs are black-box helpful for building CRHFs"). The draft's page citations are PDF indices and are correct.

checks.name: Openness
checks.finding: Immediately after stating it the paper writes "While we believe that Conjecture 6.1 holds, proving it seems quite challenging." I read past the citing passage: §6.2 introduces a distributional relaxation (Conj. 6.5), §6.3 a class-reduction relaxation (Conj. 6.11), and Theorems 6.8 and 6.12 (pp.31-32) derive only these two relaxations, and only conditionally on Conjecture 6.7, which is itself unproved ("The above conjecture is known in the case where F is itself a random oracle, but not when it is an arbitrary one-way function", p.31). §6.4 (p.33) gives a second, independent route conditional on a communication-complexity conjecture from BFM18. Nothing in §6, the bibliography, or elsewhere resolves Conjecture 6.1.

checks.name: Strength
checks.finding: The draft's two-clause unfolding matches the paper clause for clause. §6 preamble (p.28-29): "A primitive Q is BB helpful for another primitive P if Q is not black-box useless for P - meaning, if there exists an auxiliary primitive Z such that (Q, Z) black-box implies P, yet Z does not black-box imply P"; the abstract (p.1) gives the same. Negating Definition 3.2 (p.11) with Z the set of all primitives yields exactly the draft's statement. "Fully" is preserved (Conj. 6.1 says "fully black-box helpful"; the paper's other flavors are semi and forall-exists-semi, Def. 2.3). No strengthening, no weakening, no generalization.

checks.name: Quantifiers and parameters
checks.finding: This is where the draft could most easily have gone wrong and did not. The intro on p.7 states the goal in the weaker forall-F-exists-Z form: "we would need to show that for any one-way function F there is a primitive Z, which although on its own is insufficient for building CRHFs, together with F can be used to build CRHFs." The draft does not copy that ordering; it uses exists-Z, with the fully-black-box reduction of Def. 2.2 (p.9) quantifying over every implementation of the joint primitive, which is what Def. 3.2 negated actually gives. The joint-primitive breaking relation (adversary is a pair, disjunction of the two break relations) reproduces Def. 3.1 (p.11) exactly. Note the paper itself flags the exists-Z / measure-one-per-F gap on p.32 as the reason no universal primitive can be extracted.

checks.name: Attribution
checks.finding: Conjecture 6.1 is the harvested paper's own conjecture, stated in its own numbered environment and announced in its own abstract; it is not a problem attributed to someone else. Borrowed results are credited as borrowed in the draft: Simon's separation [Sim98], the IR89/Fis02 gray-zone example (p.29), the OWPF-to-CRHF construction [HL18] (p.7, p.31), the BRO combiner [BFM18] (p.7, p.33), class reductions [Sha20] (p.32), reduction taxonomy [RTV04] (p.9). All seven bibliography entries match the paper's reference list (pp.33-37) in authors, title, venue, and year.

checks.name: Definitions
checks.finding: The paper contains NO definition of collision-resistant hash functions. Section 2.2 "Specific Cryptographic Primitives" (pp.10-11) defines only one-way functions (Def. 2.6), key agreement (Def. 2.7), and (approximate) IO (Def. 2.8); I enumerated every Definition environment in the document (1.1, 2.1-2.8, 3.1, 3.2, 4.11, 6.2-6.4, 6.9, 6.10) and none defines CRHF. The draft nonetheless supplies a CRHF definition with concrete parameters (key in {0,1}^lambda, input in {0,1}^{2lambda}, output in {0,1}^lambda), placed among genuinely quoted definitions, which pins down a compression ratio the paper leaves generic. Secondary: the draft's OWF primitive "has as implementations all functions F" is a reconstruction - Def. 2.6 (p.10) defines an OWF as an oracle-aided PPT machine relative to an oracle and never spells out F_OWF, though the paper does write "F in F_OWF" on p.31. The draft's "Definition (Fully black-box helpfulness)" is also not a numbered definition in the paper; only the distributional version (Def. 6.4) and class version (Def. 6.10) are formalized.

checks.name: Fabrication
checks.finding: Four assertions not supported by the paper: (i) the invented CRHF parameters above; (ii) "the first natural inhabitant of the gray zone" / "the first natural example" - p.29 says only "a natural (and important) example", and §6.4 on p.33 already claims "a relatively natural example of an idealized primitive which does not black-box imply CRHFs, yet is BB helpful for CRHFs", so "first" contradicts the paper's own text; (iii) "The compiling-out separations and the transcript-sampling separations treated elsewhere in the paper do lift to uselessness" - p.29 says these techniques "can be fully or partially adapted", and the sampling-based KA results (Thms 4.1, 4.9, 4.12) lift only for unbalanced, perfectly-correct, or one-round protocols, with general KA left open (p.7, p.13); (iv) "Because a single conjecture about Simon's oracle cannot be pushed through for arbitrary primitives, the paper also formulates two relaxations" - an invented causal claim; p.29 gives the reason as Conj. 6.1 being hard to prove, and the actual obstruction the paper records (p.32) is that the measure-one set of Z-implementations depends on F.

checks.name: Self-containment
checks.finding: A reader who has never seen the paper could tell what to prove from the formal statement plus the supplied notation and definitions: exhibit an auxiliary primitive Z, a fully black-box reduction of CRH to (F,Z), and an argument that no fully black-box reduction of CRH to Z exists. The one caveat is that, because of the invented CRH parameters, what such a reader would set out to prove is slightly more specific than what the paper poses. No paper-internal cross-reference is left dangling in the statement itself.

corrections.problem: Presented among the paper's genuine definitions, but the paper defines no CRHF at all - Section 2.2 (PDF pp.10-11) covers only OWFs (Def. 2.6), key agreement (Def. 2.7), and (a)IO (Def. 2.8). The concrete parameters (key in {0,1}^lambda, input in {0,1}^{2lambda}, output in {0,1}^lambda) are the drafter's, and they fix a compression ratio the paper leaves open.
corrections.corrected: State CRH generically - the primitive of keyed compressing hash functions, an adversary breaking H if it finds a collision under a random key with non-negligible probability for infinitely many lambda - and add an explicit note that the paper leaves the syntax and compression parameters unspecified, so any standard instantiation is intended. If concrete parameters are kept for readability, label them as the drafter's instantiation, not the paper's.

corrections.problem: "has as implementations all functions F" is not stated in the paper; Def. 2.6 (PDF p.10) defines an OWF as an oracle-aided PPT machine relative to an oracle O, with security against PPT adversaries and negligible advantage.
corrections.corrected: Keep the break relation (it is the correct negation of Def. 2.6's negligibility requirement, and Def. 2.2 does quantify over arbitrary functions A), but note that F_OWF as a set of implementations is a reconstruction from the paper's usage "F in F_OWF" (p.31) rather than a definition the paper gives.

corrections.field: setting_latex / informal ("the first natural inhabitant", "the first natural example")
corrections.problem: The word "first" is not in the paper, and it contradicts §6.4 (PDF p.33), where the backdoored-random-oracle example is itself offered as "a relatively natural example of an idealized primitive which does not black-box imply CRHFs, yet is BB helpful for CRHFs."
corrections.corrected: "a natural (and important) example of a primitive which does not black-box imply another primitive, yet is black-box helpful for it" (PDF p.29), dropping "first".

corrections.field: setting_latex ("The compiling-out separations and the transcript-sampling separations treated elsewhere in the paper do lift to uselessness")
corrections.problem: Overstates the paper. PDF p.29: the techniques "can be fully or partially adapted to the black-box uselessness setting." The transcript-sampling lifting is restricted - Thm 4.1 needs perfect correctness plus an unbalanced construction, Thm 4.9 needs constant-round imperfect KA with constant OWF queries, Thm 4.12 covers one-round Merkle-type protocols - and general KA is explicitly left open (pp.7, 13).
corrections.corrected: "The compiling-out separations lift to uselessness in full (Thms 5.6, 5.7); the transcript-sampling separations lift only partially, giving uselessness of OWFs for perfectly correct unbalanced, constant-round imperfect, and one-round key agreement, with the general case left as an open conjecture."

corrections.field: setting_latex ("Because a single conjecture about Simon's oracle cannot be pushed through for arbitrary primitives, the paper also formulates two relaxations of the conjecture")
corrections.problem: Invented rationale. PDF p.29 gives the reason as "While we believe that Conjecture 6.1 holds, proving it seems quite challenging. Towards getting a better understanding of its plausibility, we introduce two natural relaxations." The specific obstruction the paper does record is different: on p.32, "the measure 1 of implementations Z in F_Z needs not be the same for every F, which is the reason why we cannot extract from this proof a universal primitive."
corrections.corrected: "Because proving Conjecture 6.1 seems quite challenging, the paper formulates two relaxations to gauge its plausibility - one using distributional black-box reductions, one using class reductions in the sense of Shaltiel - and shows both follow from the amplification conjecture. The distributional route falls short of the full conjecture because the measure-one set of auxiliary implementations depends on the one-way function, so no universal auxiliary primitive can be extracted; restricting to efficient one-way functions is what recovers a single implementation via Borel-Cantelli."

fabrications: The concrete CRHF syntax and parameters in definitions_latex (key k in {0,1}^lambda, input x in {0,1}^{2lambda}, output in {0,1}^lambda): the paper contains no CRHF definition anywhere - Section 2.2 (PDF pp.10-11) defines only OWFs, key agreement, and (a)IO.

"the first natural inhabitant of the gray zone between separation and uselessness" and "would give the first natural example": PDF p.29 says only "a natural (and important) example", and §6.4 (PDF p.33) already presents the backdoored-random-oracle case as "a relatively natural example" of the same phenomenon, so "first" is both unsupported and in tension with the paper.

"The compiling-out separations and the transcript-sampling separations treated elsewhere in the paper do lift to uselessness": PDF p.29 says these techniques "can be fully or partially adapted"; the transcript-sampling results lift only under restrictions (unbalanced/perfectly-correct/constant-round/one-round key agreement) and general key agreement is left open (PDF pp.7, 13).

"Because a single conjecture about Simon's oracle cannot be pushed through for arbitrary primitives, the paper also formulates two relaxations of the conjecture": an invented causal explanation; the paper's stated reason (PDF p.29) is that Conjecture 6.1 is hard to prove and the relaxations probe its plausibility, and the technical obstruction it actually records (PDF p.32) is that the measure-one set of auxiliary implementations depends on the one-way function.

"The primitive F of one-way functions has as implementations all functions F": not stated in the paper; Def. 2.6 (PDF p.10) defines a one-way function as an oracle-aided PPT machine relative to an oracle, and F_OWF is only ever used, never defined.
verify.reason: Conjecture 6.1 is on PDF p.29 verbatim, the paper calls proving it \"quite challenging\", and nothing in §6.2-6.4 or the appendices resolves it - only two relaxations, both conditional on the unproved Conjecture 6.7 - so the problem is genuinely posed and genuinely open, and the draft's exists-Z quantifier order correctly follows Conjecture 6.1 rather than the looser forall-F-exists-Z phrasing on p.7. The single most important defect is that the paper never defines collision-resistant hash functions at all - Section 2.2 defines only OWFs, key agreement, and (a)IO - yet the draft supplies a CRHF definition with invented concrete parameters (key lambda, input 2lambda, output lambda) sitting among the paper's genuine definitions, which pins down a compression ratio the paper leaves generic. Three further assertions in setting_latex are unsupported: \"first natural example\" (contradicted by §6.4), the flat claim that transcript-sampling separations lift to uselessness (the paper says \"fully or partially\", and only under restrictions), and an invented rationale for the two relaxations. Each is precisely repairable, so the draft is salvageable rather than unfaithful.
